newsitem.title: UK: Spain's gas use set for rapid growth - ministry.
newsitem.headline: Spain's gas use set for rapid growth - ministry.

text.p: The inauguration on Monday in Cordoba of the Spanish section of the Gazoduc Maghreb-Europe (GME), the pipeline carrying natural gas from Algeria to Spain and Portugal, marks a period of rapid expansion in Spain's gas industry, a top official said on Tuesday.

Maria Luisa Huidobro y Arreba, Director General of Energy at Spain's Ministry of Industry and Energy, told an industry conference here that gas currently accounts for 7.5 percent of Spain's energy balance, but that this will rise to 12 percent by 2000.
That was still well below the European average of 18 percent, she added.

Algeria will supply Spain with 10 billion cubic metres (bcm) a year through the GME initially, Huidobro said, of which 2.5 bcm will be shipped to Portugal. The GME will eventually supply Spain with more than 50 percent of its gas supplies.

The rest will come from Norway through a pipeline via France, opened in 1993, or in the form of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) under contract from Algeria, and eventually from Nigeria and Trinidad and Tobago.
Spain has LNG receiving terminals at Barcelona, Huelva and Cartagena. Huidobro added that Spain has also bought LNG from Australia and Abu Dhabi on a spot basis.

But the potential for future gas penetration in Spain is limited by infrastructure, Huidobro said. "Natural gas is not yet integrated. Andalucia is still building a network, but Extemadura and Galicia have not even begun their connections to the grid".

Spain is opening its gas supply market, and has already introduced third party access and liberalised supply to many big consumers, including electricity producers, she said. "Now we want to continue within a framework of European agreements".
She said that Spain is largely happy with discussions on the European Union's gas directive at the European Energy Council's last meeting in Brussels on December 3.

The meeeting raised the balance between public service obligations (PSO) and competition; increased transparency in the industry by unbundling of accounts; third party access to pipelines; and problems rising out of long term take-or-pay contracts which are common throughout Europe.
"The Spanish position is the the PSO/competition balance seems acceptable as it takes into account the need to establish public service provisions while at the same time allowing competition.

"As for transparency, we support unbundling of production, transmission and supply, but we want to introduce measures to preserve commercially sensitive information. And the financial burden of unbundling on smaller companies must be recognised".

With regard to third part access, Huidobro said "Spain is fully in favour of opening the market, but gradually". She said access must take into account differences between producers and non-producers, as well as the degree of interconnection between different countries.

And within Spain, different parts of the country need different degrees of protection, she added. "We could open mature parts, such as Madrid, Catalonia and the Levante, but not Galicia and Extremadura which are effectively emerging markets".
